newsitem.title: USA: U.S. condemns IRA attack, says imperils peace talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. condemns IRA attack, says imperils peace talks.

text.p: The United States condemned an IRA missile attack on Northern Ireland's Courts of Justice on Monday and warned that such incidents could complicate multi-party peace talks sheduled to resume later this month.
Washington also urged all sides to "show restraint and give peace negotiations a chance to succeed."

"The United States condemns in the strongest terms the attack on the Belfast courthouse today," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said, noting that the attack followed several discoveries in recent days of apparent Irish Republican Army bombs being prepared for "terrorist attacks."
"These incidents have shaken the fragile peace in Northern Ireland and continued violence could complicate the multi-party talks which are scheduled to resume later this month," he said.
"The United States shares the hope expressed by the British and Irish governments that these incidents will not provoke (Protestant) loyalist groups to end their cease-fire," Burns said.

The "propelled recoilless improvised grenade (PRIG)" -- part of the IRA's armory of home-made weapons -- was fired from a car passing the heavily protected court complex, the heart of Britain's legal system in the region and regarded by the guerrillas as a prestige target. A policeman was wounded.
The attack was widely seen as a further blow to lingering hopes that the IRA might call a cease-fire in the run-up to a general election that Britain must hold by May at the latest.
Britain says the IRA must restore its ceas-fire, called in 1994 but broken in Feb. 1996, to win a seat for its Sinn Fein political arm in peace talks that began last June.

On New Year's Eve, IRA guerrillas dumped a 1000 lb (450 kg) car bomb in the grounds of Belfast Castle. Police said it was intended to cause "mass murder" among security forces called to deal with the device, which was later dismantled.
Earlier IRA gunmen wounded a Protestant politician's police bodyguard and there have been recent cases of bombs being found and attacks foiled by security forces.

Protestant extremists, who have fought to keep Northern Ireland linked to Britain, are suspected of two retaliatory attacks on senior Republicans and Monday's missile raid added to fears of a backlash by "Loyalist" militants.
But Gary McMichael, a leader of the political arm of the Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF), a banned Loyalist guerrilla group, insisted its two-year-old truce was still in operation.
